title: The Kettle That Outlived Three of Its Inferiors. A Craft Report
body: The kettle in my kitchen is twenty years old. It is dented on the left flank where it met a tile floor in 2011, the handle was re-attached with a stainless bolt and a washer in 2016, and the whistle lost its cap somewhere around 2019, so now it sighs instead of shrieking, which everyone in this house agrees is an improvement. I write this as a craft report, because macrame taught me that the difference between a tool and a product is whether it can survive being loved. The economics first, as a craftperson keeps books. In those twenty years, this kitchen has hosted three electric kettles that arrived as gifts or bargains. Each died within four. One by a switch that forgot its purpose, one by a seam that wept onto the counter, one by a plastic taste that no amount of vinegar would evict. Three kettles in twenty years is one every 6.7 years; the steel veteran has therefore already outlasted its expected replacements and shows every sign of outliving me. Its lifetime cost so far is its original price plus one bolt. The cheap ones were not cheap. They were rentals with a disposal fee disguised as a purchase. But the deeper lesson is in the dents, and here the knot work speaks. A macrame piece that has hung on a porch for two years darkens where the sun reaches and stays pale where the wall shaded it. Beginners see damage; anyone who has kept anything sees biography. The kettle's dent records a morning I still remember. The bolt records the afternoon I stopped being a person who throws things away and became a person who fixes them, a promotion that cost one hardware-store visit and changed my relation to every object I own. An object with biography teaches you its material. I know now how this kettle heats, where it pours honestly, how much it whistles for one cup versus four. A new kettle every seven years would keep me a stranger to my own kitchen. The craft law I have distilled from this, and applied to cords, containers, and clothes. Buy for the repair you are willing to perform. A thing you cannot imagine fixing is a thing you will eventually discard in annoyance. A thing with a visible, simple mechanism, a bolted handle, a replaceable cap, a seam you could re-sew, invites the relationship that keeps it alive. The sighing whistle cap. I could order a replacement part. I have chosen not to, because the sigh tells me the water is ready in a voice that has become the kitchen's own, and there is no listing online for that. The honest costs, so this does not read as preaching. The old kettle is slower than a new electric one by about ninety seconds per boil. Over twenty years that is a genuine amount of standing around. I have come to treasure the standing around, the two minutes at the window while the water gathers itself, which is the only meditative practice I have ever kept for two decades. Your mileage may genuinely differ; that is allowed. And steel conducts heat in ways that demand respect around children, which the plastic ones never taught. Count the kettles of your last twenty years. If the answer is one, you already know everything in this report. If it is three or more, the next time one dies, consider the bolt. Find the oldest, simplest, most repairable version of the thing, and start its biography. Twenty years from now, someone will write about its dent.
